'''Werner Landgraf''' (born 29 July 1959, in [[Mainz]]) is a German [[astrophysicist]] and a discoverer of [[minor planet]]s.

== Life ==

W. Landgraf studied physics at the [[University of Siegen]] in 1977 and was working on his first astronomical projects.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uni-siegen.de/fb7/didaktik/sternwarte/sternwarte200401.pdf | title=Siegener Universitäts-Sternwarte| language=de}}</ref> His earliest work was very inspired by [[Brian G. Marsden]] and Victor Shor. Two years later, he joined the Department of Astrophysics of [[University of Göttingen]]. There he presented his thesis ''The calculation of atmospheric models and line profiles for the analysis of stellar spectra''. He graduated from the university in 1983,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu//full/1984MitAG..61..119./0000123.000.html|title=1984MitAG..61..119. Page 123|website=articles.adsabs.harvard.edu}}</ref> and then he worked until 1988 on his dissertation ''Nongravitational forces of Comet Halley'',<ref>{{cite web| url=http://gso.gbv.de/DB=2.1/PPNSET?PPN=630187614| archive-url=https://archive.today/20120716121004/http://gso.gbv.de/DB=2.1/PPNSET?PPN=630187614| url-status=dead| archive-date=July 16, 2012| title=Nichtgravitative Kräfte beim Halleyschen Kometen}}</ref> under supervision by [[Hans-Heinrich Voigt]].

In 1986, W. Landgraf received a teaching position at the University of Siegen. In addition to the main lecture about astronomy and astrophysics, he gave lectures also on solar system objects and their motion, Relativity and Cosmology.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu//full/1991IAUTA..21..187W/0000196.000.html| title= Summary: Report of IAU Commission 20| page=196}}</ref>

== Work ==
W. Landgraf's work mainly concerns the verification and determination of [[astronomical constant]]s of the [[International Celestial Reference System|reference system]], the [[Solar System model|masses of the planets]], non-gravitational forces and the verification of the [[gravity|gravitational law]] within the [[Solar System]]. He developed and improved methods for identifying and calculating the orbits of different objects in the Solar System. He busied himself in this work with numerous [[minor planet]]s with emphasis on the [[near-Earth asteroid]]s, [[comet]]s, their long term dynamics,<ref name="MPCarchive">{{cite web| url=http://minorplanetcenter.net/iau/ECS/MPCArchive/MPCArchive_TBL.html|title=MPC/MPO/MPS Archive | access-date=2023-11-05}}</ref> and with the [[Astrometry|observation]] of small planets and comets.<ref name="MPCarchive"/>

He also developed a method of eliminating systematic errors in positioning brighter comets that resulted in a more accurate prediction of the [[Comet Halley|Halley's Comet]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://articles.adsabs.harvard.edu//full/1986ESASP.250c.289L/C000291.000.html | title=ESLAB Symposium on the Exploration of Halley's Comet|volume=3|pages=289-294}}</ref> A recalculation of the path of [[Halley's Comet|Halley's comet]] to 2317 BC confirmed that the Greeks had already seen the comet on 466 B.C.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.softpedia.com/news/First-Halley-Sighting-Is-200-Years-Older-156358.shtml| title=Halley First Sighting Is 200 Years Older| access-date=2023-11-05}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/OnTheMotionOfCometHalley | title=On the Motion of Halley's_Comet EP/14.7/6184 ESTEC (1984)| isbn=979-10-90349-07-0| format=PDF}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | bibcode = 1985S&W....24...65L | title = Komet Halley: Bahnelemente und Perihelzeiten | journal = Sterne und Weltraum |volume= 24 |date=February 1985| page= 65 | last1 = Landgraf | first1 = Werner }}</ref>

He discovered seven minor planets including [[3683 Baumann]], [[4378 Voigt]] (named after Hans-Heinrich Voigt), [[9938 Kretlow]] and [[4349 Tibúrcio]] at [[European Southern Observatory|ESO]]'s [[La Silla Observatory]] in northern Chile.<ref name="MPC-Discoverers" /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.astro.uni-bonn.de/~pbrosche/aa/ma/ma02-93/ma02-6.pdf | title=Mitteilungen zur Astronomiegeschichte| language=de|access-date=2023-11-05}}</ref>

He examined the properties, [[Principle of individuation|individuation]] and interaction of [[Causal sets|causets]], which each starts from the affirmation that "[[Reality#Physical sciences|everything what exists, acts]]" as its first element and as its sphere of validity successively produces really news, not predetermined by nor contained in and linear independent from old, and that the earliest elements or occurred facts and their aftereffects appear as its internal logical, geometrical, physical properties (namely, the first and the next 1,2,4 ... elements of the same rank, represent its [[dimension]]s and corresponding primary [[Fundamental force|natural forces]]). Applied to our real world, this would suggest that successive events, world points, and their actions already would be an own ''discrete'' first dimension and producing force, corresponding to [[proper time]] (inclusive a discrete [[Invariant (physics)|variance]] and limited vality range of facts and their effects), followed by the similar [[time]]; a [[Impulse (physics)|kinematic extension]], and two equivalent [[Curvature of space|curvature-defining geometric extensions]]. This makes plausible that the dimensions of the world increase proportionally to their elementary units, in a not-localizable manner, very classically and approximately corresponding to a radiation with a wavelength of about the world's size, keeping the biggest part of the world's energy, per each elementary space inclusive at any background or surface one such photon or information and a pressure canceling the gravitational deceleration of expansion.<ref>
[https://archive.org/details/WeltUndWirkungsprinzip2.Aufl. ''Welt und Wirkungsprinzip''] (2.Aufl. 2010) : {{ISBN|979-10-90349-02-5|979-10-90349-01-8}} (pdf)</ref>

== Honours ==
In 1987, asteroid [[3132 Landgraf]] was named after him.<ref name="springer" />
